data.name: Ireland
data.summary: Ireland taxes a resident's capital gains at 31% for disposals on or after 7 October 2026 (33% before; EUR 1,270 annual exemption) and dividends as ordinary income at up to about 55% (40% income tax, 11% USC on non-PAYE income above EUR 100,000, and PRSI of 4.35% on unearned income). There is no wealth tax. Gifts and inheritances are taxed by Capital Acquisitions Tax at 33% above a lifetime threshold per child of EUR 420,000 (Group A, from 7 October 2026; EUR 400,000 before). Residents who are not Irish-domiciled can use the remittance basis: foreign income and foreign gains are taxed only when brought into Ireland, and foreign assets of a non-domiciled donor stay outside CAT until five consecutive years of Irish residence. An Irish investment company pays 12.5% on qualifying foreign portfolio dividends and 33% on gains, but extracting money bears about 55% personal tax.

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence (Irish-domiciled)
regimes.description: Resident and domiciled individuals are taxed on worldwide income and gains in the year they arise.
regimes.eligibility: Tax residence: 183 days in the tax year, or 280 days over the tax year and the previous year (with at least 30 days in each). This regime applies in full to Irish-domiciled residents; a new arrival usually keeps a foreign domicile and can choose the remittance basis instead.

capital_gains.summary: Capital gains are taxed at 31% for disposals made on or after 7 October 2026 (Budget 2027; 33% before that date, and 33% still for development land), with an annual exemption of EUR 1,270 per person (not transferable between spouses). The main residence is exempt. Gains on certain fund interests and life policies are taxed separately (PwC cites 40%; Budget 2027 reduces the fund and life-assurance rate from 38% to 35% from 1 January 2027 per KPMG). A reduced 10% rate (revised entrepreneur relief) applies to qualifying business disposals up to a lifetime limit of EUR 1.5 million.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Annual exemption EUR 1,270 per individual. Principal private residence relief.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Irish and EU-domiciled ETFs/funds: gains and distributions are subject to a separate 'exit tax' regime with an 8-year deemed disposal (rate cited by PwC as 40% for certain fund interests; Finance Act 2025 changes not verified). Ireland has no general exit tax on individuals leaving (not verified in statute).

capital_gains.rate_basis: Standard CGT rate 31% for all assets for disposals on or after 7 October 2026 (Revenue eBrief 142/26); no USC or PRSI on capital gains. Private business sale shown at 31% because revised entrepreneur relief (10%) is capped and conditional on working in the business.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Frequent trading can be treated as a trade (Schedule D Case I), taxing profits as income at up to about 55% including USC and PRSI.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: None; no indexation for assets acquired after 2002.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Domiciled residents: worldwide gains taxed as they arise. Non-domiciled residents: see the remittance basis regime.

dividends.summary: Dividends, Irish or foreign, are taxed as income at the marginal rate of 40%, plus USC of 8% (11% on non-PAYE income above EUR 100,000, i.e. an 8% rate plus a 3% surcharge), plus PRSI on unearned income (4.35% from 1 October 2026): about 55.35% at the top. Irish companies withhold 25% dividend withholding tax, which is credited. Foreign withholding tax is credited under the treaties, up to the Irish tax on the same income.
dividends.important_exceptions: PRSI on unearned income rises in annual steps each October (4.2% to 4.35% on 1 October 2026 per the tax-firm summaries; the Class K rate itself was not read on an official page). USC and the Class K rate for the year are blended across the 2026 tax year in practice; the 2026 steady-state top rate is used.

dividends.rate_basis: 40% income tax (above EUR 44,000 single / 53,000-88,000 married) + 11% USC (8% rate, plus the 3% surcharge on non-PAYE income above EUR 100,000) + 4.35% PRSI (unearned income, from 1 October 2026) = 55.35%. The 3% surcharge applies to income above EUR 100,000 only; the model uses the top marginal rate throughout, as the family's dividends are about EUR 600,000.
dividends.withholding_outbound: 25% dividend withholding tax on dividends paid by Irish companies; exemptions for non-resident individuals in treaty/EU states and companies with documentation.
dividends.treaty_network: About 75 income tax treaties, including the US and all EU states (count from general knowledge).
dividends.holding_company_notes: Modelled as the 'investment_company' structure regime: an Irish close company pays 12.5% on foreign portfolio dividends from EU or treaty-country listed companies (portfolio investor rule, s.21B TCA 1997), nothing on Irish dividends (franked investment income), and 33% on gains; extracting money then bears income tax, USC and PRSI of about 55.35% on the dividend. The 20% close-company surcharge (s.440) falls on income that is not distributed.

wealth_tax.summary: Ireland has no net wealth tax on individuals.
wealth_tax.important_exceptions: Domicile levy (Part 18C TCA 1997): EUR 200,000 a year for an individual who in the tax year is Irish-domiciled, has world-wide income above EUR 1 million, an Irish income tax liability below EUR 200,000, and Irish property worth more than EUR 5 million on 31 December. Residence is irrelevant and there is no citizenship test; Irish income tax paid is credited against it. 'Irish property' excludes shares in trading companies and trading holding companies. A non-domiciled arrival is outside it; a family that later acquires an Irish domicile of choice would normally pay more than EUR 200,000 of Irish income tax on a large income and so owe little or nothing. Not modelled as a wealth tax.

inheritance.summary: Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) is charged on the recipient at 33% on gifts and inheritances above a lifetime tax-free threshold per group. A child (Group A) can receive EUR 420,000 in total from both parents combined (all Group A benefits since 5 December 1991 are aggregated) for gifts or inheritances on or after 7 October 2026; the threshold was EUR 400,000 from 2 October 2024 to 6 October 2026. Spouses are exempt. Each person can give EUR 3,000 a year to anyone tax-free.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: Group A threshold EUR 420,000 (from 7 October 2026), a lifetime amount covering all gifts and inheritances from parents. Small gift exemption EUR 3,000 per donor per recipient per calendar year. Spouse/civil partner exempt. Dwelling house exemption for a child who lived in the home (conditions not verified).
inheritance.eligibility_conditions: In scope if the disponer or the beneficiary is resident or ordinarily resident in Ireland, or the property is Irish-situated.
inheritance.important_exceptions: A foreign-domiciled disponer or beneficiary counts as resident/ordinarily resident for CAT only after five consecutive tax years of Irish residence (and still resident at the date of the gift or inheritance); until then foreign assets passing between non-domiciled persons are outside CAT (rule from general knowledge, s. 6 CATCA 2003; statute page blocked).

inheritance.spouse_note: An inheritance taken by the spouse of the disponer at the date of the inheritance is exempt from CAT and is not aggregated (CATCA 2003 s.71; gifts s.70); civil partners are treated the same since 2011.
inheritance.gift_tax: Gifts are taxed the same way as inheritances (33% above the shared Group A threshold, aggregated for life since 5 December 1991), plus a EUR 3,000 annual small gift exemption per donor. A gift of assets standing at a gain can also trigger CGT for the donor, creditable against the CAT on the same event.
inheritance.business_relief: Business relief reduces the taxable value of relevant business property by 90% under conditions; it does not extend to businesses that consist wholly or mainly of making or holding investments (Revenue CAT manual Part 12, s.93 CATCA 2003), so neither a portfolio of listed shares nor the shares of a company holding one qualify.
inheritance.foreign_assets: Worldwide assets in scope if disponer or beneficiary is resident or ordinarily resident (subject to the five-year rule for non-domiciled persons). Foreign inheritance tax can be credited.
inheritance.domicile_rules: Scope follows residence or ordinary residence of either party; a person stays ordinarily resident for three years after leaving. Non-domiciled persons are treated as in scope only after five consecutive years of residence.

regimes.name: Remittance basis for residents not domiciled in Ireland
regimes.description: A resident who is not Irish-domiciled pays income tax on foreign investment income and CGT on foreign gains only to the extent they are remitted (brought) to Ireland. Irish-source income, Irish dividends and gains on Irish assets stay fully taxable. Inheritance tax follows the standard rules, but foreign assets of a non-domiciled family stay outside CAT for the first five consecutive years of residence.
regimes.eligibility: Irish tax resident but domiciled outside Ireland (domicile of origin abroad, no intention to stay permanently). No minimum stay, fee or application; claimed in the tax return. Must fund Irish living costs from Irish income, unremitted capital or clean capital without bringing in untaxed foreign income or gains.
regimes.duration_note: No statutory time limit: the remittance basis applies for as long as the person is Irish-resident but not Irish-domiciled. It ends if the person acquires an Irish domicile of choice (settling permanently), which becomes more likely the longer the family stays. The CAT advantage for foreign assets lasts only until five consecutive years of residence.

capital_gains.summary: Foreign gains are taxed at 31% (disposals on or after 7 October 2026; 33% before) only when the proceeds are remitted to Ireland; unremitted foreign gains are not taxed. Gains on Irish assets (including Irish-listed shares and Irish real estate) are taxed at 31% as they arise.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: EUR 1,270 annual exemption on taxable gains; losses on foreign assets are not deductible for a remittance-basis taxpayer.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: Not Irish-domiciled. The 0% rates for foreign listed securities, foreign private companies and foreign real estate assume the gains (and the sale proceeds containing them) are never remitted to Ireland, directly or indirectly; a remitted foreign gain is taxed at 31% in the year it is brought in. Gains on Irish assets are taxed as they arise.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Domicile can be lost over a long stay (acquiring an Irish domicile of choice) which ends the regime. Remitting the proceeds of a sale also remits the gain.

regimes.name: Irish private investment company (close company)
regimes.description: The family holds the portfolio through an Irish private limited company that they own (a close company). It pays 12.5% corporation tax on foreign portfolio dividends from EU or treaty-country listed companies (s.21B TCA 1997, portfolio investor rule), no tax on dividends from Irish companies (franked investment income), and corporation tax on chargeable gains at an effective 33%. Money taken out as dividends is taxed to the parents at income tax, USC and PRSI (about 55.35%), with the 25% dividend withholding tax credited. The company's shares are in the parents' estate with no business relief.
regimes.eligibility: Any Irish-resident person can form a private company limited by shares. US citizens are excluded: US CFC and PFIC rules tax the company's income currently. Putting an existing personal portfolio into the company is a disposal at market value for the individual, taxed at CGT (31%) on any latent gain.
regimes.duration_note: An ordinary company under company and tax law with no time limit; the close-company surcharge applies for as long as the company retains undistributed investment income.

structure.entity: Private company limited by shares (Irish close company) holding a family investment portfolio
structure.payout_notes: Dividends to a resident individual are taxed at the marginal rate: 40% income tax, USC 11% on non-PAYE income above EUR 100,000 (8% up to that), and PRSI on unearned income 4.35%, on the gross dividend; the company's 25% dividend withholding tax is credited (Revenue, Dividend income). The top marginal rate 55.35% is used on all of it. Each parent has own bands, so a EUR 400,000 payout split between two parents would bear somewhat less. A buy-back of shares taxed as a capital gain is not available to a pure investment company (not verified).
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Close-company surcharge (s.440 TCA 1997): 20% on the excess of the company's distributable estate and investment income (after corporation tax) over the dividends it declares for the period and pays within 18 months; no surcharge if the excess is EUR 2,000 or less. Income counted is interest and dividends including franked investment income; chargeable gains are not part of the income definition quoted in Revenue's manual. A family that pays out at least the year's investment income each year, as the reference family's spending requires, owes no surcharge. The 12.5% rate on foreign dividends requires the payer to be resident in an EU member state, a treaty country or the State, with a principal class of shares substantially and regularly traded on a stock exchange for the portfolio-investor route, and the investor to hold no more than 5%; dividends from other countries stay at 25%.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: Liquidation proceeds above the paid-in capital are a capital distribution (not verified here). Shares in the company are part of the estate at market value for CAT; business relief excludes companies whose business is holding investments (Revenue CAT manual Part 12).

dividends.summary: Dividends from Irish companies are franked investment income, exempt in the company's hands. Dividends from companies resident in an EU member state or a treaty country are taxed at 12.5% when the investor holds no more than 5% (portfolio investor rule, s.21B TCA 1997); other foreign dividends at 25%. Foreign withholding tax is credited only up to the Irish tax on the same dividend, so the 15% US-type withholding exceeds the 12.5% and the excess is lost.

income.name: Ireland

income_tax.summary: Ireland taxes a single person at 20% up to EUR 44,000 and 40% above in 2026; Universal Social Charge (USC) adds 0.5%, 2%, 3% and 8% in bands (to EUR 12,012, 28,700, 70,044 and above), so the combined top marginal rate is 48% (51% on self-employed income over EUR 100,000 with the 3% USC surcharge). Tax credits of EUR 2,000 personal plus EUR 2,000 employee or earned-income credit cut the bill by EUR 4,000. PRSI is 4.2%, rising to 4.35% from 1 October 2026.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Class S PRSI 4.2% to September then 4.35% from October 2026 (full-year blended about 4.24%), with a minimum of EUR 650 per income.ie (PwC says EUR 500; sources conflict) when income is EUR 5,000 or more. USC carries an extra 3% on self-employed income above EUR 100,000. The earned income credit of EUR 2,000 replaces the PAYE credit.
income_tax.local_tax_note: No local income tax. USC is folded into the brackets (income tax 20/40% plus USC 0.5/2/3/8% on separate bands: income tax band limit EUR 44,000; USC limits EUR 12,012, 28,700, 70,044). Tax credits (EUR 4,000 for a single employee) are not modelled and lower the tax by EUR 4,000 (about 20,000 of income taxed at 20%). Employee PRSI is the 4.2%/4.35% blended rate; no earnings ceiling was found on the opened page. USC does not apply below EUR 13,000 of income.

regimes.name: Special Assignee Relief Programme (SARP)
regimes.description: For employees relocated to Ireland by an employer, 30% of income between the threshold and EUR 1,000,000 is disregarded for income tax. For arrivals from 1 January 2026 the minimum salary is EUR 125,000 (EUR 100,000 for earlier arrivals) and the 30% applies to income above that threshold. The programme was extended to 31 December 2030. The relief lasts five consecutive years; employer certification within 90 days (late filing within 180 days gives four years starting the next year).
regimes.duration_note: Five consecutive tax years (four if certified late).

regimes.name: Stamp 0 residence (independent means) - closest to a nomad route
regimes.description: Ireland has no digital nomad visa and none planned. Non-EU remote workers' closest route is Stamp 0 permission as a person of independent means (about EUR 50,000 a year of non-Irish income and about EUR 100,000 in savings, private health insurance, no public funds). It does not explicitly authorise work, including remote work for a foreign employer. Taxation is ordinary residence-based.
regimes.duration_note: Renewed annually; does not lead to permanent residence.

succession.name: Ireland
succession.summary: A surviving spouse is guaranteed one half of the estate, or one third if there are children, and children can ask a court for proper provision. Ireland is an EU state outside the Succession Regulation. Trusts are recognised, though Ireland is not in the Hague Trusts Convention.
succession.reserved_share: Spouse or civil partner: 1/2 of the estate (no children) or 1/3 (with children); Succession Act 1965 s. 111. Children have no fixed share but may claim under s. 117.
succession.foreign_law_note: Ireland opted out of Regulation 650/2012. Irish rules apply domicile law to movables and the law of location to immovables; there is no nationality choice.
succession.trust_note: Common-law trusts apply but Ireland has not joined the Hague Trusts Convention. Discretionary trusts pay capital acquisitions tax: 6% on creation plus 1% a year. The Irish foundation company is a guarantee company, with no separate foundation statute.

assumptions: Top marginal rates apply (the family's income is far above every threshold); the 3% USC surcharge on non-PAYE income applies only above EUR 100,000, but the first EUR 100,000 is ignored. Income tax bands, tax credits and the EUR 1,270 CGT exemption are ignored.

The 2026 rates are those in force on 2026-10-16: CGT 31% from 7 October 2026 (Budget 2027), PRSI 4.35% from 1 October 2026, Group A CAT threshold EUR 420,000 from 7 October 2026. The Finance Act enacting them was not read.

The investment company is funded by the portfolio at its market value with no latent gain, and distributes at least its investment income each year (dividends declared and paid within 18 months of the period end), so the s.440 surcharge is nil. The family's spending (EUR 400,000 net, about EUR 900,000 gross of 55.35% payout tax) exceeds the company's investment income.

Foreign dividends are assumed to come from companies resident in EU member states or treaty countries whose principal share class is regularly traded, and the company holds no more than 5% of each, so the 12.5% rate applies.
The CAT Group A threshold is a lifetime amount per child across both parents; the engine applies it once per death event to three children who have taken nothing before.
open_questions: Needs an engine change: the remittance basis (TCA 1997 s.71(2)-(3) for foreign income and the corresponding rule for foreign chargeable gains, Revenue manual Part 05-01-21) taxes a non-domiciled resident on foreign income and gains only when they are brought into Ireland. The family spends EUR 400,000 a year in Ireland, so the tax depends on what funds that spending: capital the family held before arriving (not taxed on remittance) or remitted dividends and gains (taxed at 55.35% and 31%). The engine has one pot and no tracking of remitted income against clean capital, so the tax file's remittance_basis regime (foreign dividends and gains at 0, which assumes nothing is remitted) would understate the tax; no path is added. The regime also ends if the family acquires an Irish domicile of choice.

Needs an engine change: putting an existing personal portfolio into the investment company is a disposal at market value to a connected company (market-value rule for connected persons, TCA 1997 s.547, not opened), taxed at 31% on the latent gain. The engine has no asset-transfer event, so the path assumes a portfolio with no latent gain.

Needs an engine change: the Group A threshold is a lifetime amount shared by both parents' gifts and inheritances (CATCA 2003 Schedule 2), and the spouse's inheritance is exempt (s.71 CATCA 2003). Death in the model is one event for the whole family estate, so planning with lifetime gifts and the first death cannot be shown.
The investment company's annual running cost (accounts, annual return) is not in the tax file; the checks carry none.

Whether Revenue accepts the s.21B portfolio-investor rate (12.5%) for a pure investment company is not stated in its manual. At 25% the foreign dividends of the first investment-company check would bear 150,000 less the 90,000 credit = 60,000, and the annual figure would be 109,500 instead of 49,500. Re-check with an Irish adviser.

Citations I did not open as primary text: Schedule 24 TCA 1997 (foreign tax credit), s.129 and s.547 TCA 1997, CATCA 2003 Schedule 2 and s.71; the section numbers come from the Revenue manuals and secondary summaries.

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally
paths.note: Dividends are income at the marginal rate (40% income tax, 11% USC above EUR 100,000 of non-PAYE income, 4.35% PRSI: 55.35%), with credit for foreign withholding; gains are taxed at 31% (disposals from 7 October 2026). No wealth tax. Capital Acquisitions Tax is 33% above EUR 420,000 per child. The family has no Irish domicile, but the remittance basis is not a path here because the family spends EUR 400,000 a year in Ireland (see the open questions).

paths.name: Irish private investment company
paths.note: An Irish close company owned by the parents pays 12.5% on foreign portfolio dividends from EU or treaty-country payers (s.21B TCA 1997, holdings of 5% or less), nothing on Irish dividends, and 33% on gains. Extracting money costs about 55.35% in personal tax on the dividend, so the structure only defers tax on income the family does not spend. The shares are in the parents' estate at value: business relief excludes companies that hold investments. The 20% close-company surcharge (s.440) is not charged while the company distributes at least its investment income each year, as the family's spending requires.

immigration.name: Ireland
immigration.summary: EU citizens and (through the Common Travel Area) UK citizens live and work in Ireland without a permit. US and other nationals have no investor route any more: the Immigrant Investor Programme closed on 15 February 2023. The main options are Stamp 0 for people of independent means (about EUR 50,000 a year of income each, cannot work), the Start-Up Entrepreneur Programme (EUR 50,000 of funds), or an employer-sponsored Critical Skills Employment Permit. There is no digital nomad visa.
immigration.naturalisation: Five years of reckonable residence before applying, the last 12 months continuous (up to 70 days abroad allowed); good character and intention to stay. No language test. Applicants for citizenship by naturalisation are at the Minister's discretion. Stamp 0 time is not reckonable residence in the Department's practice (not confirmed on an official page in this research).
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: Ireland does not require renunciation; the other country's rules may.

routes.name: EU/EEA/Swiss free movement
routes.summary: EU citizens (and EEA/Swiss nationals) may live and work in Ireland without a permit; no registration is required.
routes.requirements: Right under Directive 2004/38/EC; no permit or registration. Permanent residence after 5 years of continuous residence (right arises automatically).
routes.family: Spouse and dependants join as EU family members.
routes.tax_note: Tax residence follows the 183/280-day tests, not immigration status.

routes.name: Common Travel Area (UK citizens)
routes.summary: British citizens (and Irish citizens in the UK) can live, work and study in Ireland without a permit under the Common Travel Area. Only UK citizens use this route.
routes.requirements: Applies to UK citizens only; no visa, permit or registration. Other OTHER passports must use a permit route.

routes.name: Immigrant Investor Programme (IIP)
routes.status_note: Closed to new applications on 15 February 2023 (announced by Minister Harris on 14 February 2023). No replacement investor route exists.
routes.summary: Residence for an investment of EUR 1 million and above; closed to new applications.
routes.requirements: Closed to new applications after close of business on 15 February 2023. Applications already lodged continued to be processed and approved projects and individuals keep status. Historic options were an enterprise investment of EUR 1 million, an investment fund of EUR 1 million, or a EUR 500,000 philanthropic donation (the donation and fund options are quoted from the programme as it ran; not re-verified on a current page).
routes.investment_options: Historic: EUR 1,000,000 enterprise or fund investment; EUR 500,000 philanthropic donation. Not re-verified.

sources.title: Minister Harris announces closure of the Immigrant Investor Programme

routes.name: Stamp 0 (retiree or person of independent means)
routes.summary: Permission to live in Ireland without working if you have about EUR 50,000 a year of your own income, a large reserve and private health insurance. Renewed yearly.
routes.requirements: Individual income of EUR 50,000 a year (a couple needs EUR 100,000 combined, one spouse can supply all of it), from pensions or readily accessible funds, not speculative investments. A lump sum for sudden large costs, comparable to the price of a house in Ireland. Finances certified by an Irish accountancy firm. Private medical insurance; no work, no public services. Apply before arriving; in-country applications are refused. Visa-required nationals also need a D Reside visa.
routes.fees_note: Registration fee EUR 300 per the Immigration Service page; visa fee extra for visa-required nationals (not sourced).
routes.physical_presence: Live in Ireland; Stamp 0 is granted for one year at a time
routes.family: Spouse can be included; combined income EUR 100,000.
routes.tax_note: Residence permission does not decide tax residence; 183/280-day test applies. Remittance basis is for non-domiciled individuals.

routes.name: Start-Up Entrepreneur Programme (STEP)
routes.summary: Residence for non-EEA founders of an innovative, scalable business, with at least EUR 50,000 of funds.
routes.requirements: Innovative business proposal approved by Enterprise Ireland / Department; EUR 50,000 of funding (sole applicant), reported EUR 30,000 for each further founder; capacity to create jobs. Two years' permission, renewable for a further three, per the January 2018 guidelines. Figures not re-verified on a 2026 page.

routes.name: Critical Skills Employment Permit (work)
routes.summary: Employer-sponsored permit for graduate-level and strategic occupations; leads to Stamp 4 and long-term residence after 5 years.
routes.requirements: Job offer of at least 2 years. Salary thresholds: EUR 40,904 (occupations on the Critical Skills list needing a degree), EUR 36,848 for recent graduates, EUR 68,911 for other eligible occupations. Fee EUR 1,000 (90% refundable if refused). Stamp 4 after renewal; spouse may work.
routes.fees_note: Employer or applicant pays EUR 1,000 processing fee.
routes.physical_presence: Work for sponsoring employer in Ireland
routes.family: Immediate family reunification via Immigration Service Delivery; spouse can work with a dependant permit.
routes.tax_note: Taxed as Irish resident if the day-count tests are met.
